newsitem.title: UK: Buoyant UK services underlines need for rate rise.
newsitem.headline: Buoyant UK services underlines need for rate rise.

text.p: Sustained strength in Britain's services sector suggests inflationary pressures are already building, underlining the need for a prompt monetary policy tightening, economists said on Tuesday. The Chartered Institute of Purchasing and Supply (CIPS) said in its monthly survey that Britain's service sector continued to show strong growth in April, with new business, employment, prices charged and input prices all increasing.
"The survey is consistent with other evidence showing robust growth in the services sector and the news on higher input prices is a bit disappointing," said Philip Shaw, UK economist at Union Plc.
"It shows there is certainly a need for a tightening in overall policy."

The survey showed the largest rise on record in average input prices. Salaries tend to form the largest part of input prices and official data have already shown average earnings pushing higher in the services sector.
The new Labour government stunned financial markets on Tuesday by bringing forward its first monthly monetary meeting to this morning from its scheduled date on Wednesday.
Markets are convinced this means the new Chancellor of the Exchequer Grodon Brown will raise interest rates when he makes a statement at 1000 GMT.
But the fall in the overall index, to 61.2 from 63.3 in March, has reassured some economists that activity is not getting out of control.

"Along with the overall business activity index, new business, outstanding business and employment all softened slightly suggsting that, while the service sector remains robust, there appears to be little danger of overheating," said Jonathan Loynes, UK economist at HSBC.
But the reading, still strongly above 50, means growth is still expanding rapidly.
"The survey showed a slight slowing in the rate of growth, but it is still very punchy. Growth at this pace is unsustainable," said David Philpotts, UK economist at Schroders.
"The main danger is that the inflation in earnings in the sector, showing up in input prices, spreads to the rest of the economy."
